entries.test: Published audits of chatbot medical answers that measure error rates alongside how confidently the answers are worded.
entries.note: This mixes a factual claim (often wrong, but confident) with a normative tail (shouldn't be trusted). Only the factual part is graded.

entries.test: National survey data (e.g., KFF or Pew polls) on what share of adults use AI chatbots for health or medical information.
entries.note: 'Large fraction' is vague, but survey shares give it a plain reading.

entries.test: Whether hallucinations, factual errors and overconfident wording are commonly documented across LLM evaluations, including medical ones.
entries.note: The 'entirely problematic in medicine' half is evaluative. The 'typical of LLMs' half is the testable part.
These are the BMJ study authors' words, quoted. Marcus endorses them by calling them 'entirely accurate'. 'Risks amplifying' states a possibility.

entries.test: Controlled studies (e.g., the Nature Medicine randomized study) showing whether lay users get poor diagnostic results from LLMs because key information never gets elicited, while the models do better when given complete information.
entries.note: The proposition leaves out his concession that LLMs 'work decently well with the information they've got'.
'Might' marks this as a possibility. It is a claim about expert use producing better results, so it is better classed as causal.

entries.test: Whether the four cited studies (BMJ, JAMA Network Open, two in Nature Medicine), published within a few months of each other, all concluded that chatbots are unreliable for unsupervised medical use.
entries.note: 'Cannot be trusted' is partly evaluative. What can be graded is whether the four studies agree.
This is a recommendation. The aside 'there will always be better models' is not captured.

entries.test: Calibration research on whether the confidence LLMs express tracks their accuracy, and whether training methods such as RLHF cause the mismatch.
entries.note: Stated in passing as an aside.
